Day 12 of the "40 Days of Transformation" program was a day of continued spiritual emphasis, reminding believers of the ongoing, irreversible changes God is bringing forth through His Word. Rev. Peter taught that transformation signifies a permanent alteration, where things like sickness, lack, or failure will not return once God brings healing, prosperity, or advancement [8].

Throughout Day 12, several key aspects were highlighted:
*   **The Power of the Word and Confession** Rev. Peter emphasized that the word of God works immediately, even if it takes time to manifest [13]. Faith declarations are a critical part of the 40 days, specifically tailored for transformation [3]. Believers were encouraged to be convinced that as they declare these words, the landscape of their lives and experiences are already changing [13]. A confession was made acknowledging deliverance from darkness, walking in God's kingdom, and commanding Satan to stop his maneuvers [13]. Another declaration emphasized God as an unlimited, unfailing source, ensuring sufficiency in all things and abounding in every good work [11]. Rev. Peter underscored that these confessions release life and should not be treated as mere familiar sayings, but spoken with understanding of their potent power [11].
*   **Spiritual Engagement** Participants were urged to fully engage and maximize every spiritual activity during the program, including prayer, studying God's Word, confessing it, giving, and personal spiritual exercises, taking these seriously [8]. Thanksgiving was a significant part of the morning session, with believers lifting their voices to thank God for His faithfulness, strength, and the testimonies of change and transformation already witnessed [1].
*   **New Experiences and Right Ways** The declarations for the 40 days include experiencing "total transformation" and "new experiences" in one's walk with the Lord by yielding to the Holy Spirit, leading to higher thoughts, noble deeds, and a work of righteousness that marks the end of one phase and the beginning of another [3][4]. This also involves pulling down strongholds, uprooting negative influences, and rising from setbacks into unprecedented breakthroughs [4]. On Day 12, a specific declaration was made for having "right ways" in various aspects of life for the upcoming year, including health, marriage, parenting, ministry, and finances [12]. Rev. Peter referenced Psalm 119:18-19, encouraging a prayer for divine insight to behold wondrous things from God's law and to cleanse one's way by heeding His Word [12].
*   **Community and Outreach** As Day 12 marked a point where many have "settled in" to the program, Rev. Peter encouraged participants to invite others daily to experience the transformation they are witnessing, emphasizing that the word of God is working "mightily" in them [18].

The overall sentiment for Day 12 was one of continuous improvement and building up, with the program "getting better and better by the day" and the changes accumulating [10][13].

turns.answer:
In "Godly Relationships - Part 2," Rev. Peter Alabi taught that marriage is a beautiful covenant designed by God, but love and romance must be actively brought into it by individuals, requiring effort, truthfulness, and a focus on serving one's spouse.

Rev. Peter emphasizes that love and romance are not inherently *in* marriage; rather, they are *in people*, and people then put them into marriage [1][12]. He clarifies that marriage itself will not automatically be romantic or loving; it becomes whatever the couple makes of it through their work together [15]. This means people must actively *learn* how to express love, especially unlearning habits from childhood where affection might not have been modeled [1][15]. He candidly states, "You don't have to be perfect to have a happy marriage. No, you only need to learn how to love your partner perfectly" [2][16]. To achieve this, he advises focusing more on what your partner expects from you and working on that, rather than fixating on your own expectations of them [16].

A foundational principle for marriage is to seek the interest of your spouse more than your own, fulfilling the law of God for marriage (1 Corinthians 7:33-34) [10][14]. Rev. Peter warns against "self love," calling it a "doctrine from hell" and a "satanic way of thinking" for a born-again believer, as the love of Christ compels believers to love, care for, and sacrifice for others [10].

Entering marriage requires readiness—emotional, financial, and spiritual—because it is a covenant that will intermingle and alter two lives [14]. He clarifies that the statement "two are better than one" (Ecclesiastes 4:9) is not a promise, but a hypothetical ideal that only works when both individuals actively "walk it" [12]. Marriage is described as one of the most beautiful experiences in life, despite potential negative experiences some may have had [11].

Addressing challenges in marriage, Rev. Peter highlights that marital issues demand serious wisdom and are usually case-specific; generic advice can be damaging [6][18]. He advises that marital counseling should ideally be provided by ministers who know the specific couple and their marriage, warning against applying generic online advice to unique situations [18]. He and his wife share a burden to strengthen marriages and pre-marital relationships, intending to offer teachings and platforms to deepen understanding of God's Word on these matters [6]. He also notes that a woman has "natural powers" to calm her husband, provided he is a godly man, especially when he might withdraw during confrontation [13].

The HCM 2026 messages taught that enlargement and spiritual growth come through diligent engagement with God's Word and Spirit, active discipleship, and a steadfast commitment to one's divine calling, all while maintaining joy and gratitude.

Rev. Peter Alabi emphasizes that we are called as ambassadors for Christ, sent to bring the joy of salvation to the world, recognizing that God has included us in His plans and called us to serve Him [2][13]. He teaches that diligence with our calling is a scriptural command, requiring effort and dedication (2 Peter 1:10, 2 Timothy 2:15) [7]. The core of this ministry is preaching the gospel of Jesus Christ, which is the power of God unto salvation (Romans 1:16-17) [13]. He encourages believers to value their place in God's house and understand that whatever God has called and enabled them to do is perfect for them [18].

Regarding spiritual capacity, Rev. Peter explains that spiritual tools for hearing God's voice are simple and available to all, and the manifestation of the Spirit is given to every person (1 Corinthians 12:7) [1]. He instructs us to learn how to use these tools daily in quiet time with the Lord, and to be comfortable making mistakes as we learn, because maturity is about flexibility, not being faultless [1]. He also highlights the power of praying and singing in tongues (1 Corinthians 14:15), noting that it precedes understanding and helps us access things in the spiritual world, awakening us to God's purposes [6].

Rev. Peter further teaches that we should not be driven by emotions, but by the Word of God, choosing to rejoice in the face of challenges. When emotions of sadness try to creep in, we should adjust our spirit by speaking and singing in tongues, which will bring forth songs of praise and joy, dispelling sorrow [4][17]. This joy is fixed and comes from the permanent and irreversible victory of the cross [17]. Guest minister Victor Adeyemi underscores this, stating that everything in ministry must be according to the Word of God [3] and that the church is both a house of the Word and a house of the Spirit [14]. He also notes that God can open spiritual eyes to see into the spirit realm, even for those not in the prophetic office (1 Corinthians 12) [11].

Guest minister Gbeminiyi Eboda shares that the enlargement of the church stems from the enlargement of individual members. God desires us to have a seat where decisions are made, influencing policies and outcomes [10]. He stresses the importance of mentorship, likening it to "every Ruth has a Naomi, every Joshua has a Moses, every Esther has a Mordecai" [10]. While God grants us what we need, we must still be prepared to fight for it, as everything in God's plan is worth pursuing (Deuteronomy 2:24) [16]. Challenges are meant to convince us we lack what it takes, so it's vital to recall God's past faithfulness, remembering that He is "I AM" (John 8:56, 2 Corinthians 1:10) [16]. He encourages believers to continually grow in knowledge, emerging wiser each time they engage with scripture [10], and anticipates that HCM 2026 will bring investment in light, refreshing, answers, and guidance, with our cups overflowing by its end (Psalm 118:27, Psalm 115:12) [12].

Pastor Funlola Alabi charges attendees to expect personal divine encounters and spiritual shifts at HCM 2026 that will mark their lives, ministries, callings, and works forever, leading to increased conviction and visions of enlargement [5].

Finally, Rev. Peter teaches on honoring God, explaining that true honor involves giving priority to God's affairs, such as setting aside tithes and offerings first, not after all other expenses. He reminds us to remember God as the source of our power to get wealth (Deuteronomy 8:18) [8].

turns.answer:
The Vision Sunday 2026 message, delivered by Rev. Peter, focused on understanding, articulating, and actively pursuing God's specific direction for the year, ensuring life is lived with purpose rather than by happenstance [1][3].

Key aspects of the message include:
*   **The Importance of Writing the Vision** Rev. Peter emphasized the command to "write the vision and make it plain upon tables" (Habakkuk 2:1) [5][7]. Writing what God speaks is crucial because spiritual things can fade from memory over time. This practice ensures exactness, preventing error, alterations, or a complete departure from what God originally said [5][7].
*   **The Vision Board as a Tool for Faith** The vision board is presented as a "faith thing" where individuals are encouraged to paste pictures and words representing the things God has spoken to them [2]. Regularly looking at this board—every morning before going out and every evening before bed—and giving thanks to God for its fulfillment helps combat discouragement, especially on days when progress seems slow [2].
*   **Agreement within Families** For families, Rev. Peter stressed the importance of sitting down together to review vision boards, ensuring that the visions of spouses and children align. This is vital because "can two walk together except they agree?" (Amos 3:3) [4][8].
*   **Evaluation and Numbering Days** Believers are encouraged to evaluate what God did for them in the previous year (Genesis 13:14), confronting both successes and areas where things didn't come to pass, to understand hindrances [8][15]. Numbering the days is about recognizing their significance and making the most of opportunities, walking wisely and redeeming the time (Psalm 90:12, Ephesians 5:15-18) [3][14].
*   **God's Positioning and Personal Posturing** Rev. Peter taught that God's positioning for an individual or the church should determine, influence, and inspire their posturing. This means aligning actions and mindset with what God has declared, rather than following trends [9][12]. For instance, if God says one will own properties, one should begin to posture like a landlord and engage with property-related discussions [12].
*   **Receiving Help and Helpers** Every vision requires help and helpers. Rev. Peter led the congregation in prayer for help and helpers to come "day by day," citing David's experience in 1 Chronicles 12:22, until they become "a great host like the host of God" [1][10][11]. This help extends to commitments, finances, ministry, and all areas of life [11].
*   **Wisdom and Strength** Prayers were offered for divine wisdom, which bridges the gap between potential and reality, enabling the actualization of the vision (James 1:5) [6]. Strength—spirit, soul, and body—is also vital, to run without weariness and walk without fainting, moving "from strength to strength" (Colossians 1:11) [17].
*   **Prioritizing Giving** The message also highlights giving as the first step on the vision board, emphasizing the need to prioritize the kingdom of God. Believers are admonished against making decisions that put themselves in the place of God over their lives, which can prevent them from seeing "God-sized things" [12][18].
*   **The Year's Declaration** The overarching theme and declaration for the year is "Full and overflowing," rooted in the idea that increasing faith brings enlargement (2 Corinthians 10:15-16) [2][13]. This aligns with the broader "decade of rising" that began in 2020, where God is repositioning people and new faces are emerging [16].

turns.answer:
Pastor Funlola Alabi's message, "The Book of Ephesians - Part 11," focuses on the profound transformation believers experience in Christ and their call to live a life of good works as God's workmanship.

Pastor Funlola teaches that believers were once "dead in trespasses and sins" due to Adam's fall, but through Jesus Christ, they have received eternal life and are now "alive in Christ Jesus" (Ephesians 2:1) [1][16]. This new creation signifies a complete transformation; we are God's "own handiwork, his workmanship, recreated in Christ Jesus, born anew" [2]. This new identity means that "old things are passed away" and all things have become new, making us "better in Christ than... outside of him" [14]. We are God's "masterpiece," a "work of art that is perfectly made," displaying His wisdom, power, knowledge, and intelligence [17].

While salvation is a free gift of God's grace through faith, not earned by works (Ephesians 2:8), Pastor Funlola emphasizes that believers are "saved unto good works" (Ephesians 2:10) [2][3][7]. Good works are not the price of salvation, but rather the "proof of salvation" and "evidence that we are saved," reflecting the divine nature within us [4]. They are also evidence that Jesus is alive in us [13]. These good works are part of God's eternal plan, "predestined, planned beforehand for us" [2][12].

God's grace empowers and funds these good works. When believers commit to good works, God is able to make "all grace abound towards you that you always having all sufficiency in all things you may abound onto every good work" [4][5][7]. This grace makes it easier to do good works, leading to better results and greater outcomes, and even makes it possible to prosper to meet needs [5][12]. Generosity, like Dorcas's example of making coats and garments for widows (Acts 9:36), is considered good work [5]. Primarily, the work of ministry is identified as a good work (Ephesians 4) [12].

As new creations, believers are called to not conform to the world but to be "transformed by the renewing... of your mind" (Romans 12:1) [6]. This new nature enables us to fulfill the desires of the spirit rather than the desires of the flesh, bringing peace, satisfaction, and contentment [10][18]. Every day presents a choice to satisfy either the desires of the flesh or the spirit [10][18]. Pastor Funlola also highlights that good works are proof of the "glorious togetherness" and union between the believer and the Savior, as God works in us to accomplish what He has called us to do [11][13].

He emphasizes that this verse refers specifically to "God's purpose for our lives" rather than "my own purpose for my life," noting that while they sound similar, they are "worlds apart" [1].

Rev. Peter explains that this promise stems from God's character and involvement in our lives. If God is involved in anything, there is always a purpose behind it (Romans 8:28, 2 Timothy 1:9) [9][18]. He stresses that God is only good (Psalm 73:1), and His plans for our lives flow from His love for us [4][6]. God's motives and His word are pure [7].

A significant aspect of Rev. Peter's teaching on Romans 8:28 is that God can use even negative experiences for His purpose. He clarifies that God does not cause evil, but He can certainly use evil that happens to you [6][9]. For instance, even when someone changes to become bad, like Judas, if God brought that person into your life, their actions will still work for your good because "whatever God's hand is on will work for his purpose" [5]. God has the ability to take such situations, adjust them, and make them fit into His ultimate design for your life [5].

Furthermore, Rev. Peter highlights the role of the Holy Spirit in aligning with God's purpose. The Holy Ghost helps believers to pray according to God's will (Romans 8:26-27), and it is this prayer, done in partnership with God and His will, that He then works out for our good [2]. He reminds us that "we are assured and know that God, being a partner in their labor, all things work together and are fitting into a plan for good to and for those who love God" (Romans 8:28, Amplified Classic) [16].

To walk in this truth, Rev. Peter encourages believers to "consider your ways" (Haggai 1:7) to ensure alignment with God's plan and purpose, and to consider God's word, as His plans are revealed through it [4][7]. He also points out that God's involvement is characterized by four things: pattern, process, principle, and purpose [9][18].

Yes, that's right. Rev. Peter and the other ministers at Heritage of Faith Church teach that "without faith it is impossible to please God," referencing Hebrews 11:6 repeatedly [1][3][4][5][6][7][8][9][10][12][14][15][17][18].

Here's more on what the messages teach about this central truth:

*   **Faith is God's Organ of Pleasure** Pastor Funlola Alabi teaches that faith is how we approach God, emphasizing that it's not just about *what* you bring, but *how* you bring it. If your words are not words of faith, they are not pleasing to Him. If your actions are not acts of faith, they are not acceptable [3]. Rev. Peter adds that to believe God is pleasing in His sight, and unbelief, conversely, displeases God (Hebrews 3 and Hebrews 4) [1][11]. God specifically swore in wrath against a generation that did not believe Him, showing that unbelief displeases Him [11].

*   **Faith is Required to Come to God** Hebrews 11:6 also states that "he that comes to God must believe that He is, and that He is a rewarder of them that diligently seek Him" [1][5][7][8][9][12][17]. This means acknowledging God in every area of your life is an act of faith. If you do not acknowledge God over your business, job, or marriage, you are not operating in faith in that area [12].

*   **Faith is Necessary for Salvation and Righteousness** You cannot be saved without faith [4][5][9][17]. Ephesians 2:8 (and Romans 4:16) confirms that "by grace are ye saved through faith, and that not of yourselves, it is the gift of God" [4][5][17]. Rev. Peter also teaches that without faith, it is impossible to be righteous or justified (Romans 5:1-2, Genesis 15:6) [11].

*   **Faith Enables Walking with God and Living the Christian Life** Without faith, believers "can't walk this Christian walk successfully" [4]. As Galatians 2:20 and 2 Corinthians 5:7 indicate, we live and walk by faith, not by sight [4][7][8][9]. You cannot even exist as a believer without faith [7]. Faith makes possible what has never been possible before [6].

*   **Faith is Essential for Receiving from God** Rev. Peter emphasizes that you cannot receive from God, including miracles or the ministry of the Spirit, without faith (Galatians 3:5) [9]. You also cannot pray and get results without faith [14]. Mark 11:24 teaches to believe that you receive what you desire when you pray, and Matthew 21:22 reinforces that "all things whatsoever you shall ask in prayer believing" you shall receive [6][14]. Prayer must be done in faith to be effective (James 1:5) [14].

*   **Faith Responds to God's Word** Faith is always a response to something God has said; it is not initiated by us. As Romans 10:17 states, faith "comes by hearing" [10]. When Abel offered his sacrifice, it was an act of faith because he was responding to something God said, believing God is a rewarder. His obedience was called faith [10].

*   **The Origin of Faith** The faith that pleases God is the faith God supplies [18]. Jesus is the author and finisher of our faith (Hebrews 12:2). It is God's faith given to us that becomes our personal possession. God Himself operates by this kind of faith; He doesn't see things before He believes them, He speaks and expects manifestation [18]. This is why He is called a "faith God" [18].

turns.answer:
Rev. Peter teaches that Mark 11:23 is a profound demonstration of how faith works, emphasizing the power of spoken words and the absence of doubt in the heart [1][16]. This verse says, "Verily I say unto you, whosoever shall say to this mountain, be thou removed, and be thou cast into the sea; and shall not doubt in his heart, but shall believe that those things which he saith shall come to pass; he shall have whatsoever he saith" (Mark 11:23) [1][4].

Here are key aspects of his teaching on Mark 11:23:

*   **Literal and Spiritual Application** Rev. Peter clarifies that when Jesus spoke these words in Mark 11:23, He was referring to a literal mountain standing there [3][8]. However, the principle applies to both spiritual and physical "mountains" in our lives [3]. A guest minister, Pastor Funlola Alabi, explains that "this mountain" suggests a challenge that is close by and visible, one you can directly address and overcome [7].
*   **The Primacy of Saying** Jesus mentioned "saying" at least twice as much as "believing" in this verse [4]. Rev. Peter emphasizes that speaking is even more crucial than believing because "the speaking helps the believing" [4]. Your heart is designed by God to believe what it hears from your mouth, making what you say to yourself and to the situation incredibly powerful [4]. There is no silent faith; faith always speaks [4].
*   **Believing in the Heart** While speaking is emphasized, belief is still very important [4]. You must not doubt in your heart but believe that what you say will come to pass [1][4]. When you speak to a mountain, you must believe what you are saying [9]. If something you said didn't happen, it's often because you didn't believe what you said [9]. Another guest minister, Tokunbo Adejuwon, highlights that believing occurs in the heart, not just the head (Romans 10:10, Proverbs 3:5) [14].
*   **The Power of Confession** Faith works by saying what you believe [9]. This includes not only speaking to "mountains" but also meditating on God's Word to school your heart into faith [9]. Rev. Peter encourages believers to declare, "I can move the mountain! I can do all things through Christ who strengthens me!" [10][12].
*   **The "Faith of God"** Mark 11:22, which precedes verse 23, instructs us to "have faith in God." Rev. Peter teaches that this literally means "have the faith of God" [3]. This "God-kind of faith" is made available to every believer the moment they receive Jesus as Savior [11]. It's the same faith that spoke the world into being and can work on both small and big challenges [3][11].
*   **Universality of Faith** Jesus said "whosoever," which means faith works for anyone—men, women, children, people of all backgrounds—because God is no respecter of persons (Acts 10:34, Romans 2:11, Romans 10:12) [18].
*   **Unbelief as a Hindrance** In other contexts, Jesus' disciples sometimes couldn't achieve desired outcomes because of their unbelief [2][5]. Unbelief stops the flow of God's power [2][5]. Even faith as small as a mustard seed can move mountains if there is no unbelief [2][5].

Rev. Peter demonstrates that Mark 11:23 is not just a theoretical statement, but a practical guide for how believers can operate in faith to overcome obstacles and transform their lives through spoken words, believing hearts, and the God-kind of faith [1][16][17].

*   **The Believers' Ministry** Rev. Peter explains that when John 3:16 says "God so loved the world," it refers to "men in the world," not the system of the world. He contrasts this with 1 John 2:15, which warns against loving the world and the things in it [2].
*   **The Gospel of Salvation - Part 7** Pastor Funlola Alabi invites listeners to open their Bibles and read John 3:16-19 together, highlighting that condemnation is a choice, and eternal life is a decision [3][13].
*   **The Authority of the Believer in Prayer I** Rev. Peter states that belief, as seen in John 3:16, is the way to receive the authority given to believers. He stresses that unbelief is the "greatest cardinal sin of man" and that believing in Jesus not only justifies but also grants access to power [4].
*   **The Justified Ones** Rev. Peter explains that John 3:16 represents God's invitation to all men for everlasting life, which is found only in Christ. He clarifies that God has "offered" eternal life, making it a choice, not something automatically forced on everyone [5].
*   **The Book of Colossians (The JESUS-Only Epistle) - Part 2** Rev. Peter notes that John 3:16 demonstrates God's love for "the world" (sinners), while also clarifying that a true believer's love for other saints should take priority [6].
*   **Power of the Spirit 4 - 2nd Service** Pastor Funlola Alabi points to John 3:16 as a good starting place to understand God's love, which is unconditional and everlasting, and because of this love, the power of God is available for use [7].
*   **30 Reasons Why Healing Is GOD's Will 2** Rev. Peter connects John 3:16 with John 3:14-15, explaining that Moses lifting the serpent in the wilderness was a foreshadowing of Jesus being "lifted up" so that whoever believes in Him should not perish but have eternal life [8].
*   **Persuaded** Pastor Funlola Alabi affirms that John 3:16 is a "potent" and important scripture, despite being popular, and should never be taken for granted as God's declaration [9].
*   **A Supernatural Life - Midweek Apostolic Service** Rev. Peter mentions that John 3:16 is found in John's Gospel chapter 3 and playfully suggests that if someone doesn't know it, their "particulars of salvation" might need checking [10].
*   **Armed and Trained 7** Rev. Peter teaches that every believer should be able to explain John 3:16, starting with simple questions like "Who gave? God gave." He also warns against moving to complex doctrines before understanding foundational truths like John 3:16 [12][15].
*   **The Life of GOD 1** Rev. Peter references John 3:16 as a popular verse, emphasizing that life is found only in the name of God's only begotten Son. He gives an assignment to memorize John 3:14-18 [14].
*   **Corrections and Adjustments for Transformation** Rev. Peter cites John chapter 3 as making reference to the heavens opening and the Spirit descending during Jesus' baptism [16].
*   **HCM 2025** Rev. Peter illustrates a point about sound doctrine by referencing John 3:16 [17].
*   **The Anointing** Rev. Peter cites 1 John 3:1, but also mentions the importance of reading your Bible and praying every day, implying that understanding scriptures like John 3:16 comes from such practices [18].

turns.answer:
Rev. Peter teaches that the "inward man" in 2 Corinthians 4:16 is the real you, your spirit, which is renewed day by day and is being strengthened by the Holy Ghost [1][15].

Here's what is taught across the messages:

*   In **The Things of the Spirit - Part 3**, Rev. Peter explains that the inward man, referred to in 2 Corinthians 4:16 and Ephesians 3:16, is your spirit, the "real you." He contrasts this with your physical body, which is just a "frame" or "physical house" where the real you lives [1]. He emphasizes that while the outward man may perish, the inward man is not decaying or deteriorating but is "getting stronger, stronger. Day by day, waxing boulder" (Luke 2:40, Proverbs 4:18, Psalm 84:7) [7]. He connects praying in the Holy Ghost to building up yourself on your most holy faith (Jude 1:20), which strengthens your spirit man [1].
*   In **The Lordship of the Word in the Things of the Spirit - Part 2**, Rev. Peter further describes the inward man, linking it to the "hidden man of the heart" (1 Peter 3:4) and the "inner man" (Ephesians 3:16). He states this inward man is "you, the spirit," which animates your body. He teaches that when you got saved, your spirit—the real you—was already renewed and complete, a new creation, while your soul is in the process of salvation, and your body is not yet saved [2][4].
*   In **New Creation Realities**, Rev. Peter teaches that the inward man is renewed day by day because it "is made and constituted of that spirit of eternal life." This means the inward man "cannot wax old" and does not experience the effects of the fall. Instead, eternal life is characterized by "freshness, nimbleness, agility," and "no depreciation" [14].
*   In **The Book of Ephesians - Part 16**, Rev. Peter reiterates that the inward man is renewed "by the Holy Ghost strengthening" (Ephesians 3:16). He explains that in the realm of the spirit, there is no aging, and the quality of eternal life "never deteriorates" but "remains fresh forever" [15].
*   In **Building Convictions (40 DOT 2024 Day 14)**, Rev. Peter explains that the spirit (Romans 8:16) is the inward man (Romans 7:22, 2 Corinthians 4:16), which is the real you. When born again, this spirit is exactly like God, having the same desires and preferences as God [12].
*   A guest minister, Tokunbo Adejuwon, also taught in **RFC 2025 - Day 2 Evening - The GOD-Kind of Faith** that the inward man, renewed day by day (2 Corinthians 4:16, Romans 7:22), is the "heart" or "spirit." This is because God is a Spirit (John 4:24), and He made man in His own image and likeness, so man must also be a spirit [11].

turns.answer:
Rev. Peter teaches that while "tithe" is a term many churches use, Heritage of Faith Church often refers to it as "partnership offering," which is a believer's chosen percentage of income set aside to support the work of the ministry [3][6][14].

He explains that giving to the work of God, or partnership, is distinct from "arms giving" to beggars, which God also honors but is not the same as supporting the spread of the gospel of Jesus Christ [1]. For Heritage of Faith Church, this partnership is taken very seriously [4]. Rev. Peter emphasizes that a genuine commitment to the church and the gospel is shown through one's giving, not just through vocal affirmation; "if money is not involved, commitment is not involved" [1].

Regarding the amount, Rev. Peter teaches that the partnership offering is a percentage of your income that you choose yourself [6]. While the Old Testament believers gave 10% as tithe, even without the Holy Spirit, New Testament believers, with the Holy Spirit, are encouraged to do at least 10% and ideally more [3][6]. He notes that once you increase your giving beyond 10%, it's no longer just a "tithe" [8]. Your partnership offering could be 10%, 15%, 20%, or more of your income [14][15].

Crucially, the decision of *what* to give should come from God's instruction, a "revelation" laid in your heart, rather than being pressured by man or simply mimicking what others give [14][15]. While *whether or not you will give* is a command, *what you give* is between you and God [15]. Giving is an act of free will, just like salvation [6].

Rev. Peter stresses that the mindset behind giving is vital. He shares that some consider tithe not as something given, but as returning to God what already belongs to Him [2][9]. As believers, we are bought with a price, and God owns us; therefore, our lives and possessions are not our own but His [5][10]. We are called to think as stewards, not owners, of the money in our possession, doing what God wants with it according to His Word [10]. Faithfulness in managing "unrighteous mammon" (material things) is how God proves us and entrusts us with "true riches" [9].

The primary place for a believer's generosity to the Kingdom of God is their local church, "where you are fed" [3]. Honoring God first with your partnership opens you to further guidance from Him about how to manage the rest of your money [4]. If God is not Lord over your finances, He is not truly your Lord [4]. For business owners, Rev. Peter advises acknowledging God with their substance by letting the business itself tithe from its profits, separating personal finances from business finances, and paying themselves a fair salary [11].

Every year, Rev. Peter encourages believers to talk to God about their "giving profile" and to consider increasing their giving [8][14]. He states that if you act on what God tells you to give, your harvest is sure and there will be supernatural manifestation [15].

In a related message, Pastor Funlola Alabi also spoke about Abraham giving tithes to Melchizedek before the law, demonstrating an understanding that God was his source of wealth (Genesis 14:18-20) [7].

turns.answer:
The messages from Heritage of Faith Church do not teach about "holy goats baptism." It appears there might be a misunderstanding, as the teachings distinguish between the Old Testament practice involving goats and the New Testament experience of the baptism of the Holy Ghost.

Rev. Peter Alabi and Pastor Funlola Alabi teach extensively on the **baptism of the Holy Ghost** and the **Holy Spirit**. Pastor Funlola explains that the baptism of the Holy Spirit is for everyone who believes in Jesus and can be received wherever one is. She recounted her own experience of being filled with the Holy Ghost and speaking in other tongues during a service many years ago [1]. Rev. Peter teaches that receiving Jesus means making heaven immediately and that the day you receive Jesus, a ticket is written for you [14]. He emphasizes that you are either baptized with the Holy Ghost or you face the lake of fire for unbelief; you cannot have both [14]. Moving in the spirit and flowing with the Holy Ghost often involves speaking in another tongue and being filled with the Spirit [15]. Additionally, Rev. Peter teaches that laying on of hands, accompanied by spoken words, can direct the power of God to be released for specific purposes, such as receiving the Holy Ghost [17].

Separately, the messages discuss the role of **goats** in the Old Testament as a foreshadowing of Jesus' sacrifice. Rev. Peter explains the ancient ritual where the high priest would lay hands on a "scapegoat" (or "goat of escape"), confessing all the sins of the people onto it. By this contact and proclamation, their guilt was transferred to the animal, which was then sent into the wilderness to bear their iniquities, making the nation guiltless for a year (Leviticus 16:21-22) [3][4][5][8]. This practice, however, was merely a shadow, the best they could get at the time, because it was impossible for a goat to die and then come alive [8]. Pastor Funlola reinforces that sacrificing goats was a "futile effort" and an "insult" to think it could cleanse sin, as the blood of a lesser being cannot cleanse the life of a higher one [6]. She highlights that Jesus, being sinless and God Himself, had to become man to offer the one, sufficient sacrifice (John 1:29) [5][6][8]. Jesus was the high priest, the offerer, and the sacrifice, doing everything once to bring man into the "God class" [8].

turns.answer:
Pastor Funlola Alabi teaches that boldness is a necessity for believers, crucial for fulfilling ministry, standing before men, doing God's will, and receiving His provisions [5]. She emphasizes that this is not natural boldness, but "supernatural boldness," which is a spirit from God [5][16].

Here are key aspects of her teaching on boldness:
*   **Source of Supernatural Boldness** Supernatural boldness is given by God through His Holy Spirit [10]. It comes from fellowship with Jesus and yielding to the Holy Spirit [1][14]. The apostles Peter and John were perceived as unlearned and ignorant men, yet they spoke with boldness because they had "been with Jesus" [1][2][5][7]. When you behold the face of God, His boldness rubs off on you [7]. It is also empowered by putting your confidence in God alone, not in any other person or thing [3][9].
*   **Distinction from Natural Boldness** Pastor Funlola explains that the Greek word "parasia" means unfettered outspokenness, speaking without hindrance, being frank or blunt, and fearless [5][15]. However, she distinguishes between natural bluntness, which is saying what you think without considering others' feelings, and the bluntness that comes from supernatural boldness, which is Spirit-inspired [15][12]. Peter demonstrated natural boldness and self-confidence before the outpouring of the Holy Spirit, but he later denied Jesus, showing the limits of natural confidence [18].
*   **Expression of Boldness** Boldness is primarily seen and demonstrated through the words of your mouth—your unfettered outspokenness [10][13]. It's not just about speaking loudly or being rude, but about Spirit-inspired bluntness that indicates who and what you rely on [12]. While primarily expressed through speaking, it is also expressed through the actions and choices a believer makes in life [13].
*   **Necessity and Benefits** Boldness is essential for soul-winning, as it takes boldness to preach the gospel [1][7]. It is also needed for living a supernatural life and for receiving your spiritual and material harvest [5]. God is actively increasing believers in boldness [16]. When filled with the Holy Spirit, one can cope gallantly with dangerous situations and incite a "riot against satanic domination" [14]. When you are bold and confident, the small things you do will become big, going global, and operating on a supernatural level [4][6][17].
*   **How to Cultivate and Maintain Boldness**
    1.  **Fellowship with God:** Strong personal devotion and a vibrant prayer life are crucial. When you fellowship with God, you increase in your knowledge of Him, which makes you bolder to speak about what you know [1][7].
    2.  **Prayer:** Boldness will come in the place of prayer; you can pray for boldness, and as you pray, you become bolder to preach the gospel [16].
    3.  **Yield to the Holy Spirit:** Boldness is not a function of time or something you "muster up" through courage; it comes when you yield to the Holy Spirit [1][16].
    4.  **Deal with Robbers of Boldness:** Pastor Funlola teaches that ignorance is one thing that robs us of boldness [2]. Another significant robber of boldness is sin, which brings guilt, shame, and condemnation, thus robbing you of confidence before God and in prayer [8].

Rev. Peter Alabi teaches that righteousness consciousness is key to living a victorious Christian life, enabling believers to be bold and experience God's favor, rather than being defined by their past or struggling with sin [2][9][11][12][18].

He explains that righteousness is a gift from God, a judicial declaration that we are righteous not based on our deeds, but on what God has said and done through Christ's resurrection [3][6]. When Abraham believed God, it was counted to him as righteousness, and this is the same for us when we believe the gospel (Romans 4) [3][9]. This means that instead of God counting our iniquities, He records righteousness for us, even the righteousness we did not perform [3].

This consciousness of righteousness brings several realities into a believer's life:
*   **Freedom from Condemnation** Pastor Funlola Alabi emphasizes that there is no condemnation for those in Christ (Romans 8:1), and walking in the Spirit helps us remain aware of this. Guilt and condemnation cannot take hold of us, and we are free from sin, having been forgiven of all past, present, and future sins [1]. She adds that the blood of Jesus silences the voice of self-condemnation [5].
*   **Boldness and Assurance** Rev. Peter teaches that a righteous man is as bold as a lion [9]. This consciousness of being righteous and favored by God should make us bold towards life, marking our lives, businesses, and careers with God's favor [9][12]. This favor can even cause enemies to be at peace with us [12]. The work of righteousness brings peace, quietness, and assurance forever, which means a security and trust that gives rest of mind [15] (Isaiah 32:17).
*   **A New Identity and Purpose** We are called "Victors" by God, and our past, environment, or circumstances do not define us [2]. We are children of God, not strangers, and we are precious, not condemned [1][16]. Rev. Peter stresses that there is a higher purpose in God for a believer than merely struggling with sin, falling down and rising up [18]. We are made alive in Christ, having crucified the flesh and its affections [11].
*   **Living Righteously** While righteousness is a gift, it also entails living a righteous way [10]. Rev. Peter clarifies that "righteousness" refers not only to our right standing with God but also to our conduct. He states that "he that is righteous will do righteously" [10]. Pastor Funlola notes that good deeds, ethical actions, and virtuous behavior are expressions of our righteous nature, but they are not what make us righteous or save us [7]. Holiness, in thought, affection, desires, and passions, is the life God has called us to [11].

Rev. Peter encourages believers to live in the consciousness that they are a spirit, not merely a body, which is key to living a more victorious Christian life [14]. The blood of Jesus reaches into our conscience and cleanses us, giving us a righteousness consciousness [5]. The blood and the Spirit flow together, so wherever the blood is mentioned, the Holy Ghost moves, empowering us to resist temptation by speaking God's Word and pleading the blood of Jesus [5][11].

Rev. Peter teaches that speaking in tongues is the initial evidence of being filled with the Holy Spirit and a continuous experience for believers to exercise their reborn spirit, allowing them to flow with the Holy Ghost and unlock spiritual gifts [2][7][12][17].

Here's more about what he teaches regarding speaking in tongues:
*   **Gateway to the Supernatural and Mysteries** Speaking in tongues is the gateway to the supernatural and allows you to unravel mysteries, uncovering what was not spoken before. When you pray in the spirit, you gain a lot of knowledge [1].
*   **Initial Evidence and Continual Experience** When people are filled with the Holy Ghost, they speak with tongues as the Spirit gives them utterance (Acts 2:1-4) [2][3][8][11]. This was the first evidence that they were filled [12]. However, it is not limited to being just an initial evidence; it must be a continual experience for the rest of one's life, a flowing stream that should never dry up, and a practice that assists in the worship of God [4][7][12][16][17]. Rev. Peter thanks God that he speaks in tongues more than an entire church (1 Corinthians 14:18) [6][17].
*   **Edification and Spiritual Strength** Speaking in tongues edifies or builds up oneself on one's most holy faith (Jude 1:20) [6][7][8]. It is a way to edify your spirit man and exercise yourself in the power of God, demonstrating God's power [4][6][8][13].
*   **Unboxing Spiritual Gifts** When you pray in the Holy Ghost, all other gifts of the Spirit begin to find expression. Speaking in tongues is like the "key" that opens them up, unboxing your spiritual gifts [4]. Pastor Funlola Alabi also notes that utterance gifts, like tongues and interpretation of tongues, are manifestations of the Spirit [15].
*   **Knowing Things** As you pray in the Holy Spirit, you will know things—not only about the Bible but generally about your life, people connected to you, and events [7][16].
*   **Yielding to the Spirit** Being filled with the Holy Spirit means yielding to Him, and when you are yielded, you will speak (Ephesians 5:18, Acts 2:4) [10]. The power of God is a gift, and prayer enriches you in the use of that power, determining what it can do in your life [3][5]. You must not quench or stifle the Holy Spirit; always yield to Him when He tries to stir you up [10]. The believer is expected to be pliable and yielded to the Spirit so He can carry them beyond human limitations into the supernatural [11].
*   **Power is a Gift** The power of God is a gift; it is not earned through good works or church service [3][5]. There are no powerless Christians, only those not enriched [5].

    *   Enlargement is in God's plan and program, and He is not in the business of things remaining small (Isaiah 9:7) [9][2]. The Lord will increase you "more and more," meaning your story of increase will be unending (Psalm 115:14) [9].
    *   This expansion will spread to the right and left, and descendants will inherit nations, making desolate cities inhabited (Isaiah 54:13, Zechariah 1:17, Jeremiah 31:39) [4][2]. There will be nothing strong enough to stand in the way of God's expansion agenda for His people [2].
    *   Corporate enlargement is occasioned by individual enlargement, meaning that as individuals increase in their faith, it leads to the enlargement of their collective sphere of influence (2 Corinthians 10:15) [2][4]. Each person has the potential to become much more than they currently are; "a little one shall become a thousand" (Isaiah 60:22) [2].
    *   God wants His people to grow, and the church provides an opportunity to develop emotional intelligence and grow in love work (1 Corinthians 13:4-8) [13].
    *   Being connected to the "head" (pastors) is crucial because whatever progress comes to them indicates what will happen to you; the anointing flows from the head down (Psalm 133:1-2, Colossians 2:19) [15][16].
    *   Heritage of Faith International Church will be like towns without walls, expanding beyond measure due to the multitude of people and God being a wall of fire around it (Zechariah 2:1-5) [17].
    *   This is the "favor clock" and "enlargement hour" in your life, so don't give up on the eve of your coronation (Lamentations 3:31) [4].

turns.answer:
Rev. Peter teaches that faith comes by hearing the Word of God, specifically the message of Christ, and that continuous hearing is essential for growing stronger in faith [6][14].

Here’s more from the messages:

*   In **Stronger in Faith 4- First Service**, Rev. Peter explains that faith comes by "hearing the thing preached," which is the message of Christ's death, burial, resurrection, and ascension. He emphasizes that just as faith comes by hearing, it grows stronger by continuous hearing [6]. He also points out that Jesus repeatedly commanded, "He that has ears to hear, let him hear" (Matthew 11:15, Matthew 13:9, Matthew 13:43, Mark 4:9, Luke 8:8, Luke 14:35) [6].
*   In **RFC 2025 - Day 1 Evening - 5 Elements of Faith**, Rev. Peter states that hearing is the first and crucial element of faith, essential for receiving it and for sustaining it (Colossians 2:6). He notes that the Israelites in the wilderness lacked faith because they heard the word but "didn't listen to the word," "didn't want to hear it," and "rejected the gospel message," therefore "they could not receive the faith of God" [14][18].
*   In **Day 16**, Rev. Peter teaches that faith comes by "hearing and hearing the thing preached," which refers to the word concerning Christ and the gospel of salvation. He says that the gospel carries faith with it when it is heard [5].
*   In **Faith, Foolishness and Presumptions or Fear - Part 5**, Rev. Peter clarifies that if faith comes when we hear the word, then exposing ourselves to more of God's Word will make faith take a stronger hold on us. He contrasts this with fear, which comes from hearing the word of Satan [9].
*   In **Day 3**, Rev. Peter explains that faith comes only by hearing the word of God, specifically "the word about Christ" (Romans 10:17). He adds that even after faith has come, one needs to know how to release it through "corresponding action" that aligns with the word heard [2][16].
*   In **Second Service**, Rev. Peter states that faith comes by hearing the message of Christ, specifically "the good news about Christ" concerning God raising Him from the dead (Romans 10:17) [10].
*   In **Our Heritage of Faith 1**, Rev. Peter teaches that the faith needed for salvation is supplied by the gospel itself when a man hears the gospel message, imparting the faith of God into his spirit (Romans 10:17) [4].
*   Pastor Funlola Alabi, in **HCM 2025**, also teaches that faith comes by hearing the word of God, describing the word as "the vehicle that carries faith and conveys it into the heart of man." She explains that this is how faith came for salvation, and it is how faith is quickened to receive what we desire [1].
*   Pastor Funlola, in **Faith Essentials**, emphasizes that "if there's no word of God, there is no faith" (Romans 10:17), distinguishing between natural human faith and the faith of God [3][13].
*   Pastor Funlola, in **RFC 2025 - Day 1 Morning**, explains that the faith of God is a gift received "through the hearing and the believing of the word of God" (Romans 10:17) [8].

How to be led by the Spirit of God

In *How to Build Lasting Relationships*, Andrew Eluwa states that when you are in a church and you see something as a problem, you should be aware that you are somehow supposed to be part of the solution [1][2]. He gives an example of noticing cobwebs in the church or people not being greeted, and says that if you notice these issues, you should do something about them rather than just observing [1]. He emphasizes that knowing what is good and not doing it is considered sin [1][2]. He also advises that when acting as a church member or worker to address a problem, you should "never go in your name" [1][7].

turns.answer:
In *How to Build Lasting Relationships*, Andrew Eluwa taught several other important principles for living and relating within the church and beyond, in addition to being part of the solution.

He emphasizes that believers have not come to serve man, but to serve God. He notes that everyone cannot be like you, and you should not allow someone else's actions or inactions to deter you from your God-given possession [8]. Hiding your gifts in the church is presented as a disaster in faith, because the natural tendency for anything not used is to be lost or to disintegrate. He likens it to a house or car left idle, which begins to crack and mess up, highlighting that staying idle anywhere you find yourself leads to problems [8] (Matthew 25:14-30).

Andrew Eluwa also shared insights on communication and handling grievances. He teaches that if you have a point regarding an issue, you should go directly to the leader or whomever you have access to in authority, rather than publicly demotivating people [4][9]. He explains that talking is not the problem, but who you are talking to and how you are talking matters. Your words must be seasoned (Colossians 4:6), ensuring the person receiving it understands. He advises adding wisdom and virtue to your communication [9][14]. Furthermore, he states that when people offend you, they sometimes may not even realize it [2]. He notes that people often find it easier to project themselves onto others, meaning that what someone says others are complaining about might actually be their own complaint [9]. He adds that sometimes, you are the only one thinking what you're thinking, such as believing a person is wicked or a church is a certain way, when you haven't truly asked anyone else [6].

Regarding relationships, he stresses that to truly enjoy the fruit of friendship and partnership in your career, you must allow time to process both yourself and the other person [7]. He highlights the power of words, urging people to be mindful of what they say, and advising parents to never allow anyone to body-shame their children, even jokingly [7]. He addresses entitlement mentality, clarifying that while something might be "right," accessing it as a matter of right can kill gratitude. He differentiates between false entitlement and true entitlement, noting that while you shouldn't feel anyone owes you, you should recognize that you owe someone something. He also links stinginess to hindering financial or business breakthroughs [15].

Andrew Eluwa further teaches that where your heart is, there your treasure will be [5][10]. Those who lack a true stake or investment in a work will leave when difficulties arise [5][10]. He warns to be careful of people who have nothing to lose in a relationship, church, or business, as they can be dangerous [10]. Drawing from the story of Gideon, he illustrates that quality friendship and dedication are more important than quantity, as God thinned out Gideon's army to the truly committed ones, identifying those who were "unwilling and unable" [5][10][18] (Judges 7:3). He connects Jesus' growth in stature, wisdom, and favor (Luke 2:52) to the importance of physical well-being through diet and exercise, as the body is needed to function in this realm [13]. He also encourages seeking answers and asking questions, understanding that we don't know everything [6], and advises that those aiming at a mark should not pay attention to every negative remark [17]. He concludes by reminding us to rejoice with those who rejoice, and not to be intimidated or unable to be genuinely happy for others' achievements [12]. The ultimate reward for a good and faithful servant is to enter into the "joy of your Lord," which is beyond mere salary [14].

turns.answer:
Rev. Peter teaches that while "tithe" refers to 10% of one's income, in Heritage of Faith Church, this practice is encompassed within "partnership offering," a New Testament concept where believers decide a percentage of their income to give to support the work of the ministry [3][6].

He elaborates on several key aspects of giving:
*   **Definition and Mentality** Rev. Peter explains that tithe is traditionally 10% of income [6][8]. He shares a perspective from a Christian who considered tithe not as "giving," but as "returning back to God what already belonged to Him" [2][9]. This mindset acknowledges God as the owner of all things, viewing ourselves as stewards rather than ultimate proprietors [10]. This acknowledgment of God's ownership is a decision, where one declares, "Lord, this thing is yours. I am just possessing it for you" [10][11].

This partnership offering is a percentage of your income that you choose to set aside to support the work of the ministry [3][6]. This is considered a duty for every believer [6].
*   **New Testament Giving** While Old Testament believers were dictated to give 10% because they didn't have the Spirit of God within them, New Testament believers, having a reliable heart where God's love is shed abroad, are instructed to give "as God has prospered him and as himself has proposing his heart" (Romans 5:5) [8]. Rev. Peter encourages believers to do at least 10%, noting that those in the Old Testament gave 10% without the Holy Ghost, so New Testament believers with the Holy Ghost should do no less, and ideally more [3][6]. Giving in the New Testament is an act of free will, just like salvation [6].

A specific, revelation-based offering (e.g., 5,000 or 10,000 naira per service) leads to supernatural manifestation, unlike giving based on transient feelings [15].

Peter emphasizes, "put your money where your mouth is" to support the spread of the gospel [1]. He teaches that if God is not Lord over your finances, He is not truly your Lord [4]. Honoring God first with your partnership offering opens you up to further leading from Him about the rest of your money [4].
*   **Business Tithing** For business owners, Rev. Peter teaches that the business itself should tithe, acknowledging God with its substance. He advises separating personal finances from business finances, with the owner paying themselves a fair salary from the business, while the business itself gives to God's work [11]. This is seen as a way to consecrate the business to the Lord [11].
*   **Purpose of Giving** Giving supports the spread of the gospel of Jesus Christ [1]. It is one of the obligations believers have in the local church, alongside serving wholeheartedly and making oneself available for training [3]. It is also linked to the principle of faithfulness, as God uses material things (unrighteous mammon) to prove a believer's faithfulness before entrusting them with true riches [9].

Rev. Peter also teaches that the church operates on a principle of not borrowing money, instead paying cash for everything and banking with God, trusting that "he who sent us takes care of us" [12]. He also stated that spiritual fathers can also give money to their sons and daughters in the faith, as an injection of blessing into their lives [13][16].

Rev. Peter teaches that while "tithe" traditionally refers to 10% of one's income, Heritage of Faith Church often refers to this practice as "partnership offering," which is a New Testament concept. This offering is a percentage of your income that you choose to set aside to support the work of the ministry, and it is a duty for every believer [1].

Here are further details Rev. Peter teaches about giving:

*   **Partnership Offering vs. Tithe:** In HHF, while the church is not against tithes, the practice is called "partnership offering" [1][3]. Rev. Peter explains that tithe is specifically 10% of income [1][2]. They prefer "partnership offering" because once giving exceeds 10%, it's no longer strictly a tithe [2]. As New Testament believers, Rev. Peter encourages doing at least 10%, and even more, because Old Testament believers who didn't have the Holy Ghost gave 10% [1][3].
*   **New Testament Giving Principles:** Giving in the New Testament is an act of free will, similar to salvation [1]. Believers are instructed to give "as God has prospered him and as himself has proposing his heart" (2 Corinthians 9:7) [2][12]. This is because New Testament believers have a reliable heart where the love of God is shed abroad (Romans 5:5), unlike Old Testament believers who had to be dictated to [2]. Your giving should reflect your financial capacity, and it's not about the size of the offering but about your faithfulness [10]. You propose the amount in your *own* heart, not based on what others give [12].
*   **Mentality of Stewardship and Ownership:** Rev. Peter emphasizes that giving stems from an attitude of stewardship, recognizing that we don't own the money we have; God owns it [4][18]. He recounts the perspective of a Christian who viewed tithe not as "giving" but as "returning back to God what already belonged to him" [4]. This acknowledgment is a decision: "Lord, this thing is yours. I am just possessing it for you" [8]. Thinking as a steward, rather than an owner, is essential for prosperity, and faithfulness in stewarding material things allows God to entrust more [14] (Luke 16:11) [4].
*   **The Purpose of Giving:** Giving generously is an obligation, and believers should give where they are fed, with their local church being the primary place of generosity to the Kingdom of God [3]. Giving is an act of faith that requires stretching yourself and believing God [12]. It is part of how the work of God gets done, and the local church is built upon the sacrifices of many [3]. God may prosper people so that resources can flow to where they should, and some people cannot be prospered if money in their hand will never flow [6]. Giving can also be for the kingdom, which should be the first thing on your vision board [2]. Creating real wealth is necessary to sustain charity and missions [9].
*   **Practical Aspects of Giving:** Rev. Peter teaches that giving is a doctrine of the New Testament and must be taught [12]. He advises having a specific amount for your regular offering in every service, rather than giving randomly, as this helps with planning [12]. For business owners, he stresses separating personal and business finances as a matter of faithfulness. A business, as its own entity, should also tithe from its profits as a way of consecrating it to the Lord and acknowledging God with its substance [8].

Pastor Funlola emphasizes that salvation is purely by grace through faith, a free gift of God, and not a result of any works or human striving (Ephesians 2:8) [1][2][4][5][8][9]. She cautions against teachings that suggest salvation is earned by works, or "Jesus plus something," clarifying that such messages are a misleading counterfeit that twist the true Gospel of Christ [2][12]. The price for salvation has already been paid by Jesus, making it a gift that requires no further payment or works to maintain [5]. Our redemption, justification, righteousness, and acceptance in Christ are all gifts from God [8].

She explains that good works are not the price we pay to be saved, but they are the *proof* and *evidence* that we are saved [6]. These works demonstrate that we have received the divine nature of God, who Himself does good works; just as God looked at His creation and declared it "very good," so too when believers do good works, they are proving to be like their Father [6]. Examples of such works include forgiving others and acting with generosity, reflecting God's giving nature (John 3:16) [6]. Pastor Funlola succinctly states, "The believer is not saved as a result of good works, but good works are the result of salvation" [6].

Pastor Funlola shares that good works are an essential part of God's plan for believers. In Ephesians 2:10, it states, "For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God has before ordained that we should walk in them" [4][9][13]. This scripture, she teaches, summarizes a believer's salvation and assignment, revealing a purpose that was predetermined from the foundations of the world before anyone was made [4][7][9]. She states that what believers are doing now is *discovering* what those good works are, not defining them, and this discovery comes from the scriptures [13].

She teaches that these good works are "works of grace," which makes them easier, possible, and leads to better, even super-abundant results [3]. Grace empowers believers to achieve greater outcomes and accomplish things in record time [3]. The primary good work God has called believers to is the work of ministry [3][7][13]. She highlights that Jesus Christ exemplified this, spending His earthly years doing good works of ministry, going about doing good and healing all oppressed by the devil (Acts 10:38) [13]. Every believer has been "saved to be sent" and called to be a "preacher of the word," which doesn't necessarily mean becoming a pastor, but actively participating in spreading the Gospel [7][9][10].

turns.answer:
Rev. Peter Alabi teaches that good works are not the means by which a person achieves salvation or earns God's approval, but rather they are the natural outcome and an ordained purpose for believers who have already received salvation by grace through faith.

He clarifies that salvation is a complete and perfect job done by God, not something we can contribute to or add to through a holy life or good deeds [13]. Salvation is a sovereign act of God, purely of God, and was His eternal plan, not an answer to human prayer or effort (1 Timothy 2:4-6) [18]. We are saved by grace through faith, and this is a gift of God, "not of works, lest any man should boast" (Ephesians 2:8-9) [10]. He stresses that acts of righteousness cannot save us (Titus 3:5), and no man is justified by the deeds of the law (Romans 3:20, Galatians 3:11) [10].

However, Rev. Peter emphasizes that while our works do not save us, our salvation *produces* good works [10]. He states, "For we are his workmanship created in Christ Jesus unto good works" (Ephesians 2:10) [10]. This means that we are saved and ordained to do good works [10][15]. He cautions against two extremes: one that says "we don't do anything" because "Christ alone" has accomplished everything, and another that tries to add to what Christ has already done [10]. Christ alone means we don't do anything *in addition* to or to *accomplish* what He has already done [10].

The *motive* behind good works is crucial. If the intention is to make God love or accept us, then it is no longer a good work [10]. Instead, we do good works to honor God, not to get His approval or earn forgiveness, because we are "already been accepted in the beloved" [16]. Good works are also a way to open ourselves to receive rewards from God [16]. He illustrates this by noting that two Christians, born again on the same day, might experience more benefits from God if one is "exercising himself to the things of God" [16].

Furthermore, Rev. Peter assures us that God has before ordained good works for us to walk in, and our future is secure, even when we make mistakes. He suggests that God has factored our human proclivities into His plan, weaving even wrong turns in such a way that it appears as if they were orchestrated by God, ultimately turning out right [15]. Our authority in Christ, he reminds us, is not given on the basis of our good works, so we should not allow the devil to use our perceived shortcomings to silence us from exercising that authority [5].

turns.answer:
Rev. Peter teaches that marriage, at its core, is not inherently filled with love or romance, but rather these qualities are brought into it by the individuals involved, making it a dynamic partnership built on conscious choices and spiritual principles [3][15][18].

He emphasizes that the amount of love and romance in any marriage directly correlates with the effort and intention the couple puts into it [18]. This perspective counters the idea that love is found automatically within the institution itself [3][15]. The love of God, which Christians are called to emulate, is characterized by giving without expecting anything in return (Romans 5:8) [14]. Therefore, a marriage works best when "two givers meet, not two takers or one giver and one taker" [14]. Rev. Peter teaches that husbands are to love their wives (Ephesians 5:25) and wives are to submit to their own husbands (Ephesians 5:22), seeing this as the counsel of the Lord [15].

For building strong companionship, Rev. Peter highlights several key elements:
*   **Devotion:** Married individuals must be devoted to their spouse, constantly thinking about how to please them (1 Corinthians 7:32-34) [6].
*   **Commitment:** This involves taking responsibility to nourish and cherish your spouse, much like watering a plant (Ephesians 5:29) [1][6]. It means sticking to what you have said and staying faithful to your word [2].
*   **Preference:** You must prefer your spouse above all others, including parents, siblings, friends, and colleagues [1]. This preference demonstrates honor, which Rev. Peter notes is mutual in marriage (Romans 12:10, 1 Peter 3:7) [1]. He also warns against exhibiting a "hard-heartedness" or being "without natural affection" towards one's spouse, as described in 2 Timothy 3:3, urging believers to be kind, tenderhearted, and forgiving instead (Ephesians 4:32) [6].

Rev. Peter strongly teaches that marital relationships are bound by exclusivity; it is not permissible to bring a third party into a marriage, nor to have "open relationships" as a believer [4]. Furthermore, he states that marriage is not "by Bluetooth"; it demands a commitment to live together physically—in the same space, sleeping on the same bed, and eating from the same table [13]. While temporary separations for work may occur, they should never become permanent, as prolonged physical distance will cause the marriage to suffer by allowing the couple to grow apart [13]. He also emphasizes that in marriage, "there is no me. There is no I. It's we and us" [9].

Unity and agreement are crucial for a couple living by faith, as disunity is dangerous [5]. The ability to fulfill marital instructions, such as submission and love, is rooted in being filled with and yielding to the Holy Spirit (Ephesians 5:18) [5]. Pastor Funlola Alabi also teaches the importance of marrying another believer to ensure spiritual growth together, mutual prayer, and accountability, which she considers true "couple goals" over superficial displays [8]. A guest minister, Sola Babalola, added that there must be an "agreement" between the husband, wife, and God, and that both spouses have a responsibility to understand and honor each other, and to change for the sake of the marriage, working towards a shared purpose [12].

Rev. Peter advises intelligence in the use of words, discouraging negative confessions in marriage vows like "for better, for worse, in sickness and in health." Instead, he encourages couples to say, "I will stand with you in all seasons of life no matter what," emphasizing the underlying intent of communication [2].

He also encourages couples to see their spouse not just romantically, but as a "destiny team" and partner in purpose. He urges prayer for an enlightening of the heart to perceive one's spouse correctly in the light of God's calling, which he believes will lead to more effective, fruitful, and productive partnering [7].

Rev. Peter stresses the importance of seeking God's counsel in marriage, affirming that it is the counsel of the Lord for husbands to love and wives to submit [15]. He advises that any new relationship that harms existing, healthy relationships is a "bad sign" [16]. He also offers strong counsel that "it's never too late to be right," even if it means stepping back from an impending marriage minutes before the altar, assuring support for such decisions [16]. He teaches that it is better to "win the heart of your husband or your wife than to win argument," as a focus on winning arguments can lead to losing the marriage [17].

Rev. Peter teaches that for singles, the period before marriage is a crucial time for personal growth, setting righteous standards, and preparing for a godly relationship, rather than simply waiting for a spouse [1][7][10][13].

He stresses that singles should not be pressured into marriage if they are not ready [1][16]. Readiness for marriage involves being emotionally, financially, and spiritually mature [1]. He emphasizes the need to be true to oneself and not force readiness that doesn't exist [1].

For those who are single and looking to marry, Rev. Peter advises to "shine your eyes" and "look well before you leap" [1][3]. He reminds singles that courtship is not marriage, but a time to prepare for it [7]. During courtship, individuals should not try to eliminate their uniqueness or suppress their true personality to please someone else [7]. Instead, it's a time to celebrate who they are [7].

He offers key guidance for singles:
1.  **Build yourself:** This involves growing up personally and spiritually [10][13]. A "grade A Christian" marrying another "grade A Christian" leads to a healthy marriage [13]. Focus on personal growth and developing relational skills, becoming a "Rolls-Royce" that is sought after rather than always seeking [18].
2.  **Set and live by righteous standards:** These standards should be based on God's Word, not societal norms, especially when seeking to marry another Christian, as these standards will be common to both [10].
3.  **Develop relational skills:** Be deliberate about the quality of relationships, identifying those that pour into your life and avoiding parasitic ones [18]. Relationships should draw you closer to God and bring out the best in you [18].

Rev. Peter also teaches that the idea of a single "chosen one" is not scriptural, reminding us that God's plan is not limited by one person's life or death [4]. He affirms that God can inspire decent, romantic songs that minister health into marriages and courtships, guiding singles to live with purity and enjoy their courtship [5]. He also states that romance, as commonly understood, does not exist in the realm of the spirit, and that if it is the love of Christ, it is enough for any marriage and relationship [6]. He encourages singles to understand that marriage is not compulsory [3].

turns.answer:
Rev. Peter teaches extensively on divine healing, emphasizing that it is God's will and an active reality available to believers today through various avenues.

He states unequivocally that God desires for us to live a full and healthy life, and sickness is a ploy of Satan to terminate a calling [1]. God can give new organs, or repair existing ones, as He wants us to live a full life [1]. The healing power of God is verifiable, not "fabu" [1]. God's word is explicitly referred to as medicine (Proverbs 4:20-22), and it's impossible for His word to be medicine if healing isn't His will [13]. Furthermore, God promises to bring "health and cure," not just a reversal of illness (Jeremiah 33:6) [4].

Rev. Peter outlines several avenues through which healing is received:
1.  **Laying on of hands:** This is a direct avenue for receiving healing [2]. When ministers lay hands on the sick, they shall recover [15].
2.  **Prayer of faith:** The prayer of faith saves the sick, and the Lord raises them up (James 5:14) [2]. There are also specific "preemptive prayers" which are a spiritual warfare strategy, where you pray over things the devil hasn't even done yet [17].
3.  **Ministry gifts:** God ministers healings through spiritual leaders, often referred to as elders [2]. The "gift of healings" is a specialized anointing, as seen in the life of Apostle Paul, through whom God wrought "special miracles" (1 Corinthians 12, Acts 19:11-12) [2].
4.  **Faith in God's word:** Healing is received in the human spirit by faith, not primarily through the head or emotions [15]. When the power of God is acknowledged, it does what it came to do [6]. A "touch of faith," a purposeful touch, draws power from the spirit, unlike a casual or curious touch [8][11].
5.  **The presence of God's power:** The power of God is always present to heal and meet needs during services, capable of bringing deliverance and escape [5][12]. It can even bring healing "beyond what their faith can carry," helping to build faith [6].

Rev. Peter instructs believers to confess healing, commanding pain to leave, and to do things they couldn't do before as a demonstration of their healing [3][7][9]. He encourages believers to take authority over sickness in their own bodies, seeing themselves as the temple of God where no sickness can stay (1 Corinthians 3:16) [16]. He teaches that we should not tolerate sickness, but rather drive it out with the same authority Jesus used [16].

Rev. Peter's journey with the keyboard began in his youth, driven by a desire to serve God and a determination not to remain spiritually inferior [1][10].

As a young student in GSS3, Rev. Peter decided to give himself to God's word, prayer, fasting, evangelism, and learning to play the keyboard, making it one of the first things he did in his family church [1][10]. He became useful by volunteering to play, and as he grew, he didn't need to fight for places in the church because they found him to be an asset [1]. Guest minister Victor Adeyemi explains that Rev. Peter dedicated "hours and hours and hours" to learning and playing the keyboard, while also spending extensive time "in prayer and fellowship with God," ensuring he would not be merely an entertainer but a vessel for God's manifest presence [4][6].

His skill quickly developed, leading him to displace all the church's organists, and he progressed from playing at his branch to the Lagos district and eventually national events [1].

Rev. Peter recalls playing keyboard for different parishes, including one in the Redeemed church, but he found what he was truly looking for when he walked into a Rema Chapel branch [2]. He was initially paid 3,000 Naira monthly and given a pair of black shoes for playing the keyboard there about 24 to 25 years ago [3][7]. Despite the branch being "rough" and "dusty," using older equipment, and having very few members, Rev. Peter knew it was his church after hearing the Word of God preached for the first time in a way that was "just different" and revealed "the power" [2][3]. He then told the pastor not to pay him anymore, as that was where he began to learn "the things of the spirit," including all-night prayer meetings [3]. He later brought a brother to Rema Chapel to be their keyboardist, and that brother is now a minister there [7].

He also volunteered himself and his keyboard to play for other fellowships, including Dr. K of Kingsword on campus, often after exams when he had no academic reason to be at school [5][14][15]. He would do this joyfully, hoping to be blessed by the anointing of the ministry's founder or to be recognized, but he was often not noticed [5][12][15]. This experience initially bothered him, making him question if something was wrong, but the Lord revealed to him that he was sent to serve the anointing, not necessarily to meet or be acknowledged by the founders directly [12][15]. Rev. Peter learned that God's love for him was not dependent on a minister recognizing or identifying him, as a minister's "mental faculties can still escape the influence of the Holy Ghost" [12]. He also understood that people are in different seasons of life, which helped him rejoice for others' prosperity without envy, even when he served and received no material reward himself [16].

Rev. Peter also remembers trekking through places to get to church to serve and learn keyboard for Rema Chapel about 28 years ago, and during those treks, he would confess and meditate on the Word [13]. Even today, he shares that he can sit at the keyboard, and a song will flow in his spirit [8]. He encourages believers to be bold and sing with melody in their hearts onto the Lord, or to play on the keyboard if they know how, because God will show those who ask [8][18].
